- TTFT target: firm goal is <= 100 ms p95 for the majority of interactive flows (most responses 256-1,000 tokens). We can accept up to 120 ms p95 on rare cases but would want an escalation path.

- Streaming transport: SSE is preferred (simplicity in browser), but we can support WebSocket if Redwood recommends lower overhead.

Subject: Re: Intro + perf targets (TTFT & streaming) — follow-up

Jordan — great questions. High level answers and notes below; Aditya and Marcus are looped for engineering/size confirmation.

1) Can hosted API meet TTFT <= 100 ms p95 with SSE at your scale?
- Short answer: depends on model size and tokenization. For mid-sized open models we typically hit TTFT p95 in the 70–130 ms range on our Hosted fleet for 512-token responses at moderate concurrency. Hitting <=100 ms consistently at sustained 250 concurrency for 600-token responses is tight on pure shared-hosted.

2) Recommended approaches:
- Option A (fastest time-to-value): Run a short benchmark on your representative prompt set against our Hosted API using SSE. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 TTFT and token-window cadence. If the hosted numbers are within your tolerance we can proceed with a pilot.
- Option B (predictable SLOs): Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity) sized with optimized kernels and quantization profiles. With a Dedicated pool we can tune for TTFT <=100 ms p95 for your 600-token median payloads — we will need to validate with a bench run but plan is to reserve GPUs optimized for low latency (e.g., 8x A10s / 4x H100 depending on model).

3) Streaming transport and chunk cadence:
- SSE is fully supported. Our runtime can emit incremental token chunks; typical chunk cadence we recommend is 40–120 ms depending on tokenization and model. We can push sub-60 ms cadence for smaller tokens when using continuous batching disabled and aggressive flush thresholds.
- WebSocket gives slightly better control for backpressure and binary payloads if you need unified streams for multiple channels.

4) Next steps I need from you:
- Representative prompt set (5–10 prompts across lengths).
- Network egress constraints and whether the client will be in your VPC (for Private) or calling hosted endpoints from the public internet.

I attached an updated SLO-matrix with example latency buckets and suggested rollback/fallback options. Marcus — can you propose an initial Dedicated sizing and rough cost ballpark based on 250 concurrency / 200 reqs burst?

Best,
Marissa
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Jordan / Marissa — quick engineering note from the bench team. High-level assumptions and recommended starting point: 

Assumptions: 600-token median response, model ~7B–13B (float16 or 4-bit quant), SSE streaming with token-by-token flush, 250 sustained concurrency.

Estimated Dedicated sizing (initial pilot):
- 4x A10 GPUs in a dedicated pool with optimized kernels and prioritization for low-latency inference.
- With that config we expect TTFT p95 in the 80–110 ms range for the majority of interactive flows and chunk cadence ~50–120 ms depending on token sizes.
- If you need consistent <=100 ms p95 headroom at 250 concurrency under bursty traffic, consider 8x A10s or 4x H100s to reduce queuing tail latency.

Benchmark plan:
1) Acme provides 10 representative prompts and a script that mimics your browser batching pattern (SSE open connection + streaming).
2) Redwood runs 2 runs: Hosted baseline (non-dedicated) and Dedicated pilot. We’ll capture p50/p95/p99 TTFT, token cadence histogram, and end-to-end CPU/NET metrics.
3) Deliver a short report and recommendations within 5 business days of receiving the assets.

Notes on transport:
- SSE: easiest client integration; we recommend tuning server-side flush thresholds to avoid tiny-chunk storms (we’ll advise on a 40–60 ms target).
- WebSocket: use if you need backpressure control or multiplexing multiple conversational channels over one connection.

I can draft a concise pilot-run Statement of Work and cost estimate once we agree to proceed.

Thanks,
Aditya Rao
